summary: Redwood demo focused on edge-case behaviors: long-context sessions (100k+ tokens), bursty high-TPS patterns, streaming backpressure and timeout behavior. Team walked through Console live-tail, Optimize recommendations, and a simulated stress run showing graceful fallbacks and retry behavior vs. hard timeouts. Customer wants Dedicated options + pilot for production verification.
topics: Long-context/very long sessions and KV cache behavior
High concurrent TPS and autoscale & Dedicated pool sizing
Streaming backpressure and client timeout strategies
Fallback policies: model variants and region failover
Observability: per-token latency breakdowns, backpressure graphs
Pilot and next steps for Dedicated capacity
transcript:
00:00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick sound check?
00:00:05 Liam: Sounds good on my end, thanks.
00:00:08 Ethan: Great. I'll kick off with a very short agenda — demo the Console live-tail, show an Optimize suggestion set, then run a short stress scenario that reproduces the latency/backpressure you mentioned.
00:00:18 Sana: Perfect. We're especially interested in what happens when session length grows past 64k tokens, and when our ingestion bursts to 5k TPS.
00:00:25 Priya: Yeah we'll try to cover both — and show how Redwood falls back and how you can tune timeouts and retries.
00:00:32 Diego: One ask — please surface the logs where we can see client-side drops vs server backpressure.
00:00:38 Ethan: Absolutely, we'll show the live tail and also the per-route breakdown.
00:00:45 Maya: Quick housekeeping — recording on, screenshots ok.
00:00:49 Liam: Fine.
00:00:50 --- 
00:01:05 Ethan: Okay pulling up the Console — this is the route the app would call, /v1/generate-summarize in our sandbox. Notice the per-token latency heatmap here, that's new in Optimize.
00:01:18 Maya: There might be some slight mis-labeling in the transcription, we sometimes see K-V cache written as K slash V cash in the logs, ignore that.
00:01:28 Sana: ha, yep we've seen that in other tools too. So question: in long contexts do you stream the full context on every call? We usually append the full session history which can be huge.
00:01:40 Ethan: Short answer — no, we don't resend everything. There are two patterns: prefix caching and KV cache. For very long contexts we push the prefix into the KV cache so only new tokens are streamed. That keeps the network payload low but maintains model state.
00:01:57 Diego: Does that work across model variants? If you fallback to a quantized variant, will the cache still be valid?
00:02:05 Ethan: Good question. Cache compatibility is best within a family — we annotate model variants that are KV-cache compatible. If you fallback to a distil variant, you might need a cold-start. Our fallback policy can force a warmup to rebuild prefix state.
00:02:20 Liam: What's the observed latency when we hit a 120k token session and then 500 concurrent users append 2k tokens each?
00:02:30 Ethan: In our internal 100k token tests the per-token generation after warmup holds at ~18–32ms median on A100-class backends with continuous batching — but the prefix reconstruction can add a one-time 300–800ms depending on warmup strategy.
00:02:47 Sana: And when TPS spikes — say 5k TPS sustained for 30s — how does Redwood protect latency SLOs?
00:02:56 Priya: We route by policy. For Hosted customers we do smart routing by shard and model variant, and for Dedicated you get reserved GPUs with autoscale policies and burst capacity. In a surge we can degrade to a cheaper but compatible variant for a percentage of requests, or we can enqueue with backpressure signaling.
00:03:14 Diego: Enqueue meaning we delay at the router? Our concern is client timeouts — we can't block for long.
00:03:20 Ethan: Right, that's where streaming backpressure and client-side timeout strategies meet. We provide a streaming protocol where the server will emit progress frames and partial tokens; if you see increased queue time we also emit an Estimated-Start-Time header. Client can choose to wait, reduce request size, or fail fast and retry.
00:03:36 Liam: Can we see that in the live-tail?
00:03:38 Ethan: Yep — switching to live-tail demo. I'm going to kick off a synthetic load generator that simulates 3 patterns: steady 200 TPS, burst 5k TPS for 20s, and long sessions being appended.
00:03:58 --- 00:04:02 [ambient noise]
00:04:05 Maya: Running the load now — you should see new traces in the left column.
00:04:12 Sana: I see them. The queue depth spikes are already visible.
00:04:16 Ethan: See this stacked chart? The grey is queued requests, yellow is executing, red is timed-out. At 00:04:20 I flip the fallback policy to allow 30% of traffic to route to a quantized variant.
00:04:30 Diego: I see latency drop a little but token quality — how do we monitor regression?
00:04:35 Priya: We tie quality checks to prompt sets. Optimize can run a small eval set on the fallback variant and surface a delta score. If the regression exceeds your threshold we stop the fallback.
00:04:46 Liam: The transcription earlier mentioned continuous batching — can you explain how batching interacts with streaming?
00:04:55 Ethan: Sure. Continuous batching aggregates requests that are in the runtime queue up to a latency window. For streaming we do micro-batches — we stream tokens as they're produced, and batching only delays sending of the first token by a small microsecond window. That allows high throughput without blocking streaming semantics.
00:05:12 Sana: What about client timeouts? We have a 3s frontend timeout — if the server queues for 2s and then backs off another 1s warmup we cross 3s easily.
00:05:22 Ethan: Two levers: set a lower server-side request timeout and use streaming progress frames so the client sees activity; also use the Estimated-Start-Time header to let the frontend show a spinner. For UI critical paths we recommend a 500–700ms p95 tail requirement and use a smaller top-k or shorter context to guarantee it.
00:05:39 Liam: In practice do teams prefer failing fast and retrying vs waiting for server warmup?
00:05:45 Diego: We usually fail fast and re-try idempotently with jitter. We're worried about duplicate billing though.
00:05:50 Maya: Redwood supports idempotency keys on requests so retries don't double-bill for completed streams — partial streams are a bit trickier but we annotate response states.
00:06:00 Sana: Okay can we jump to the error logs where you mark backpressure reasons?
00:06:05 Ethan: Scrolling — here's an example: "queue_threshold_exceeded -> backpressure_applied -> fallback_started". You'll also see the Estimated-Start-Time and the chosen fallback variant in the trace meta.
00:06:18 Liam: Can the Estimated-Start-Time be relied on? We had a case with inaccurate EST and it hurt UX.
00:06:25 Priya: EST is best-effort and includes current queue length and average execution time for that model variant. It can be wrong during sudden topology changes, but having it is still better than nothing for UX decisions.
00:06:37 Diego: Any advice for SDKs? Our RN client is sensitive to streaming frames — sometimes frames reorder with network jitter.
00:06:44 Ethan: We recommend sequence numbers on frames and a small reassembly buffer. The SDKs do that by default; our public SDKs include reordering protection.
00:06:53 Sana: Nice.
00:06:56 --- 00:07:05 [15s silence while demo runs]
00:07:20 Ethan: Now I'm going to switch to a long-context simulation. This sim attaches a 110k token history using prefix stitching and then submits a 2k token update.
00:07:32 Liam: Watching the traces — I see a spike in warmup time.
00:07:36 Ethan: That's the prefix reconstruction. The runtime decides between rehydrating state via KV cache or reencoding the prefix. If KV cache has the session, latency is small; otherwise the reconstruction path is heavier.
00:07:48 Maya: Note: we instrument the Console to flag sessions where prefix size > 64k so you can proactively GC or archive older turns.
00:07:58 Diego: Is there a way to evict or pin sessions programmatically?
00:08:02 Ethan: Yes, there's an API to pin session state in Dedicated pools, and you can set eviction policies per-namespace.
00:08:09 Sana: For Dedicated pricing, what's the unit — GPU-hours or committed throughput?
00:08:14 Priya: It's reserved GPU pools with a committed vGPU throughput. You choose baseline capacity and optional burst. We can provide a sizing worksheet.
00:08:23 Liam: Please send that worksheet.
00:08:26 Maya: Noted as action item.
00:08:29 --- 00:08:33 [brief crosstalk]
00:08:40 Ethan: Back to streaming backpressure — I'm going to force a scenario where the router queues requests and we enforce a 1.5s server-side timeout.
00:08:50 Diego: Why 1.5s? Our front-end is 3s but we want to avoid waiting more than half that.
00:08:56 Ethan: Exactly. Watch the response stream; when queue time exceeds 900ms, the router emits Early-Terminate frames and marks the trace as backpressured.
00:09:08 Sana: I see a series of "early_terminate" events and then a retry attempt. Some clients might not honor server-suggested retries.
00:09:16 Maya: On that note — Redwood's retry policy is configurable per-route: backoff, jitter, and idempotency-key behavior.
00:09:24 Liam: We use SSO with SAML — any special considerations for Dedicated?
00:09:28 Priya: Dedicated supports SSO/SAML and customer-managed KMS. Audit logs are shipped to your SIEM.
00:09:35 Diego: Does the audit include raw prompts?
00:09:38 Priya: We support redact-on-ingest and token-level redaction. By default prompts are stored for X days; you can configure retention or disable storage.
00:09:48 Liam: Good.
00:09:50 --- 00:10:00 [demo continues; load spikes]
00:10:22 Diego: The graph just hit the red zone — I see timed-out requests.
00:10:26 Ethan: Yup — here's the fallback in action. The quantized variant picks up 25% of traffic. Notice latency improves but quality delta is visible in the eval widget.
00:10:38 Sana: How do you compute the quality delta? Is it BLEU, ROUGE, or a learnt metric?
00:10:43 Priya: It's customizable. You can upload your eval set and pick metric(s). For summarization you might use ROUGE+model-based coherence score we provide.
00:10:55 Liam: We need to avoid surprises — can you send examples of model-variant diffs on our prompt set?
00:11:00 Maya: We'll include that in the benchmark spreadsheet.
00:11:03 --- 00:11:20 [30s while run continues]
00:11:55 Ethan: All right, switching to the trace explorer — here's a path that shows repeated client retries and a final success. The trace meta shows idempotency-key: abc-123, retries: 2, reason: backpressure_imposed.
00:12:08 Diego: That helps. Question: billing for aborted streams — how is it measured?
00:12:13 Maya: Billing is per-token successfully emitted plus a small request overhead for the compute allocation. If a stream aborts during queueing we don't charge for model compute, but there's a small enqueue fee. Retries with same idempotency key won't double-bill if the original completed.
00:12:27 Sana: What's the enqueue fee like?
00:12:29 Priya: Small — it's primarily to discourage abusive patterns; we'll include exact numbers in the cost sheet.
00:12:35 Liam: Any customers with workloads like ours you can reference?
00:12:39 Maya: We have customers in fintech and health with very long contexts and bursty ingestion. We can share anonymized perf slides.
00:12:47 Diego: Great.
00:12:50 --- 00:13:05 [Demo finishes; screen share ends]
00:13:10 Ethan: Quick recap: we showed KV cache and prefix behavior, continuous batching and microstreams, fallback variants with eval deltas, Estimated-Start-Time and backpressure signals, and Dedicated sizing options.
00:13:24 Liam: That was useful. A few follow-ups: 1) send that benchmark/workbook, 2) provide Dedicated pricing and burst commitments, 3) propose pilot runbook with exact test harness.
00:13:35 Maya: All captured. We'll send an email with attachments.
00:13:40 Sana: Can you also include the SDK guidance for sequence numbers and reassembly?
00:13:45 Ethan: Yep, will include links to the RN and Node SDK streaming sections.
00:13:51 Diego: One more question — how does storage retention work for KV cache backups? We are in regulated space.
00:13:58 Priya: For Private/Dedicated you can choose customer-managed storage and encryption; we can also set retention to zero and keep only ephemeral state.
00:14:08 Liam: Good.
00:14:12 --- 00:14:30 [15s pause]
00:14:32 Maya: Ok, are there any blockers for starting the pilot?
00:14:36 Liam: We need to get security sign-off and a rough cost estimate. Also legal will want a data flow diagram.
00:14:43 Priya: We'll attach an architecture diagram and the SOC2 docs.
00:14:47 Maya: Action items — we'll send the benchmark sheet and pricing by Monday, runbook and pilot proposal by next Wednesday.
00:14:56 Sana: Sounds good.
00:15:00 Diego: Thanks everyone.
00:15:02 Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up.
00:15:05 --- 00:58:00 [call end logged]
